title: Balance between electric and acoustic instruments; amplifying the tuba
summary: Gil describes problems balancing electronic and acoustic players and plans to put a contact mic on the tuba.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: I was going to say, I was talking about this question of balance and I know that a symphony conductor definitely has to think in terms of balance with instruments and the sounds and all of that. And I don't think we have to go into that in any great detail. But in as much as there is so much improvisation in jazz do you think that you have to pay as much attention to that in creating the sound that you want?
Balance you have to think of it all the time.
You want to talk a little bit about it?

We have some problems with balance between the electronic instruments and the acoustic instruments. We are having problems with that according to where you are sitting. For example, if an acoustic player is sitting and he is surrounded by electronic instruments, it's very hard for him to put up with/you know.
Since they have all this energy which they can get with a little turn. So physically he's not capable of competing with it and psychologically he's

very, very depressed at the idea of somebody being able to, somebody being able to get energy like this rather than like this. And with all the work that goes into learning to play and acoustic instrument there's something to that. Although a very good player is not going to be, not going to labor that point or hold that kind of reason that much provided he doesn't have to be the unlucky one is competing for sound, right? And then he doesn't get drowned out by the electronics, all the time.

So I had that problem at ( ?) after we played there six weeks. Six weekends rather. Sometimes the electronic got out of hand. Or if it didn't, I never really did think it was too loud. But I didn't think that the acoustic instruments were amplified properly. And we had problems. The sound system was stolen, we had it stolen for one thing.

I'm not quite sure how I'm going to resolve that situation now. ( ?) keeping it down the way it's supposed to be. And it's a delicate think in a way too because some players don't mind putting pickups on instruments and some do. I don't know how, I'll have to speak to some of the players about it.

For example, the tuba, as large an instrument as it is, it's a very delicate instrument and it needs to be amplified when it's played in a low register, you know. I know when it's played up high and it's shouting you can hear it. But when it's played down low which you can do very beautifully and agilely and all that, it has to have a microphone. It just cannot be heard over the sum total of the decibels that come from that band.

The drum, the guitar the bass and all of that. So I will speak to Howard and ask him if he would consider clipping a little contact mic on that tuba. And it should be able to be solved by having a microphone that he can just use on his own. He can use when he wants to do it and it's going to be loud enough, you know. It can be turned up by somebody who is doing the mixing, but you can't always have those ideal situations. So, those things like that.
